title: 2026-03-04 Redwood cost-econ discovery with Parallax Analytics
summary: Intro discovery focused on cost/unit economics for text-generation at scale. Customer runs high-volume inference for summarization and trading signals; primary constraints are latency SLOs (~150ms p95), strict budget targets, and data residency. Discussed Redwood hosting tiers, batching/cache levers, reserved capacity, and next steps to run a short benchmark and share pricing model.
next_steps: Redwood: send conservative cost model + example batch sizing spreadsheet (Maya)
SE: schedule 2-hour benchmark run and share test harness (Liam)
Customer: provide sample traffic profile and 2 weeks of token metrics (Evelyn)
action_items: Maya Chen: Email pricing spreadsheet and security one-pager (due 2026-03-06)
Liam O'Connor: Provision benchmark env and share runbook (due 2026-03-09)
Evelyn Park: Share 14-day traffic dump and SLAs (due 2026-03-08)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Liam O'Connor, Priya Nair (Redwood) -- Evelyn Park, Raj Patel, Zoe Kim, Tom Alvarez (Parallax)

Summary: quick discovery on cost/unit economics and deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private); ask for sample traffic and run benchmark.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, is this a good time?
[00:09] Evelyn: yeah perfect, thanks Maya, we wanted to focus on economics mostly today, so like cost per token and levers we can flip.
[00:18] Maya: great, I'm Maya I'm your AE, Liam from infra is on the call to dig into batching and perf. quick high level, Parallax what are you running today?
[00:29] Evelyn: so we run a nightly ingest and then a near real-time summarization for trading signals. about 40 million tokens a day currently, spikes to maybe 120M at market open, and we need p95 latency under, uh, about 150 to 200 ms for the real-time path.
[00:47] Liam: got it. are you on-prem now or cloud? and any restrictions on sending data to a hosted API?
[00:55] Raj: mostly cloud; infra is on AWS in us-east-1. data residency is us-only. we can use hosted if there's a VPC/private endpoint, otherwise we'd consider Dedicated or Private.
[01:06] Maya: that makes sense. in terms of cost sensitivity, is this a fixed budget or more of a cost-per-token target?
[01:14] Tom: finance is watching unit economics closely; we have a target of keeping inference < $0.0006 per token average across workloads, otherwise it's hard to scale.
[01:24] Priya: okay, helpful. quick clarification: when you say token, is that input+output combined or just output?
[01:30] Zoe: we usually budget for total tokens (input+output) so that's the right number to use.
[01:36] Liam: cool. a few levers we usually talk about: batching/concurrency, KV/prefix caching, quantization and model choice, and reserved capacity for Dedicated which can drop unit cost. any of those you've tried?
[01:49] Evelyn: we've tried basic batching client-side but not true server-side continuous batching. we don't have prefix caching set up.
[01:56] Raj: also curious: how much does quantization hurt our output quality for summarization? small change in rouge can be bad for trading signals.
[02:05] Liam: yeah that's a fair concern. quantization can change some nuances. with Redwood our Optimize tooling suggests quant profiles by workload - e.g., 4-bit quant for high-thr cost-savings but we'd run evals on your prompt set; we recommend canarying quantized variants.
[02:22] Maya: to give a concrete example - for hosted API per-token pricing depends on model size and latency tier. for Dedicated you commit to reserved GPU capacity which brings predictable lower unit costs for steady throughput. Private has highest ops overhead but full control.
[02:36] Raj: can you share numbers? ballpark for say a 13B model vs a 70B?
[02:43] Priya: ballparks only, yes.
[02:45] Maya: sure ballpark - hosted 13B might be in the $0.0005 to $0.0009 per token range depending on fulness of batch and caching; 70B could be 2-3x. Dedicated reserved pricing can cut that by ~30-50% for steady state. exact depends on batch sizes and KV hit rates.
[03:05] Tom: ok so we're targeting 0.0006, sounds like 13B hosted might be close, but spikes will bust that.
[03:12] Liam: right, spikes are the tricky bit. two approaches: autoscale Dedicated with burst capacity or use Hosted with smart routing + fallback to smaller model at high load. Also prefix/KV caching reduces tokenization cost if many requests share prompts, and continuous batching on the runtime packs concurrent requests to improve GPU utilization.
[03:32] Evelyn: about caching - our requests are often similar, lots of overlapping context for instruments. what hit rates are realistic?
[03:39] Liam: hit rates vary - for strong prefix overlap you can see 30-60% effective token savings; for less overlap maybe 5-15%. worth running a sample to estimate.
[03:49] Zoe: how do you measure that? like what do you need from us?
[03:53] Maya: a 7-14 day traffic dump with representative requests and timestamps is ideal; SE will run analysis to simulate batching, cacheability, and token distribution.
[04:03] Raj: ok we can do that but need to scrub PII.
[04:06] Priya: also note we provide a private deployment option with VPC control plane that keeps data in your network; that usually helps compliance teams.
[04:15] Evelyn: what's the uplift in engineering to run Private?
[04:19] Priya: Private has a heavier setup and maintenance; we have an on-prem package or a VPC-managed option. engineering lift depends on scale; our customers often start Hosted or Dedicated and then move Private for compliance.
[04:31] Tom: let's focus on cost-first for now. can you walk through how batch size affects per-token cost?
[04:37] Liam: sure. smaller batch sizes increase latency and lower GPU utilization, which raises per-token cost. as batch size increases you amortize kernel startup and memory overhead. with continuous batching the runtime collects very small windows and packs them; typical sweet spot is batch sizes of 8-12 for 13B with short sequences. but that also depends on your latency SLOs.
[05:00] Evelyn: our median sequence length is about 120 tokens, tails to 800 sometimes. how would that shape recommendations?
[05:07] Liam: longer sequences reduce the effective batch throughput; we'd simulate your seq length distribution. also consider prefix caching on long tails to avoid recomputing earlier tokens.
[05:15] Zoe: what about concurrency limits? we want high QPS at open.
[05:19] Liam: Dedicated with reserved capacity gives predictable concurrency; autopilot policies can keep latency stable during spikes. Hosted can do autoscaling but billing is variable.
[05:28] Raj: you mentioned fallback to model variants - how seamless is that?
[05:32] Maya: you can configure smart routing policies - e.g., primary model is 13B, fallback to a 7B quant variant at 95th percentile load to keep SLAs. Redwood console shows per-route latency and errors.
[05:44] Tom: can we get an example cost model? something showing tokens -> cost for various batch sizes and caching hit rates.
[05:51] Maya: yes we'll send a conservative spreadsheet. it will show scenarios: hosted 13B, hosted 13B with 30% cache hit, dedicated reserved 13B with 40% cache hit, plus fallback model routing.
[06:03] Evelyn: perfect. also security - we need SOC2 and audit logs; what does Redwood provide?
[06:09] Priya: we have SOC2 reports, SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integrations for Private. I can send the security one-pager.
[06:18] Raj: do you persist KV cache on customer side or server side?
[06:22] Liam: KV cache is managed by the runtime server-side; for Private you can keep cache within your VPC. for Hosted we encrypt in transit and at rest; we can also provide options for customer-managed keys depending on the tier.
[06:36] Zoe: one more on quality - how do you guard against quantization regressions?
[06:40] Liam: Redwood Optimize runs evaluation suites tied to your prompts and can alert on quality regressions; we recommend A/B rollouts and canarying quantized models with a subset of traffic.
[06:52] Evelyn: sounds good. what about trial/pricing - can we do a short pilot?
[06:56] Maya: yes typically pilot is 2-14 weeks: we run a benchmark with your traffic, tune batch/cache, and then produce an expected cost per token and an ops runbook.
[07:05] Tom: and cost of pilot?
[07:07] Maya: usually covered as part of sales engagement for customers of this size; we'll confirm in the follow-up email.
[07:13] Zoe: ok good.
[07:16] [longer technical dive section - Raj and Liam exchange perf details]
[07:20] Raj: are you able to pin model versions for Dedicated? we need deterministic results for backtesting.
[07:25] Liam: yes you can pin model versions and rollback; we support model versioning and controlled rollouts.
[07:30] Raj: about KV memory - how do you size it?
[07:33] Liam: KV memory is by sequence length and context window; the runtime exposes metrics and we can recommend hardware (e.g., A100 vs H100) based on your tail latency and model size.
[07:45] Raj: are H100s necessary for 70B?
[07:48] Liam: for 70B and real-time SLOs H100s or similar are recommended to keep p95 low. GPUs drive kernel choices.
[07:56] Evelyn: back to economics - if we commit to Dedicated reserved 3-month minimal, what kind of delta should we expect vs Hosted?
[08:03] Maya: typical reserved commitment gives about 30% lower unit cost over hosted list; with higher commitment and larger capacity you can get up to ~50% in some cases. again exact depends on your traffic shape and cache hit.
[08:18] Tom: can you include in the model a scenario where cache hit is 40% and batching improves avg batch size to 18?
[08:24] Liam: yes we'll model that.
[08:26] Zoe: okay any blockers before you can run the benchmark?
[08:30] Maya: we need the traffic dump, sample prompt sets, and your target SLOs. SE will provide the harness and expected runtime.
[08:38] Evelyn: we'll scrub and share the data. one question: what about cost smoothing during spikes, e.g., can you buy burst credits?
[08:46] Priya: we have burst capacity and also routing policies; for Dedicated customers we can set up burst pools and priority queues to avoid huge overages.
[08:56] Raj: how are overages billed? monthly invoice?
[09:00] Maya: yes standard billing monthly; Dedicated contracts have commit tiers and overage rates.
[09:07] Tom: ok, finance wants an order-of-magnitude OPEX projection for 6 months.
[09:12] Maya: we'll include a 6-month projection in the follow-up.
[09:16] [00:09:20 - quick interrupt, crosstalk about calendar invite]
[09:30] Liam: technical note - if you have a high prefix reuse pattern we can enable sticky routing to keep hot contexts on the same GPU to maximize KV cache hits.
[09:42] Raj: sticky routing sounds good, any downsides?
[09:46] Liam: tradeoff is less balancing across GPUs which can cause hotspots; we usually combine sticky routing with autoscaling and eviction policies.
[09:55] Zoe: what's the expected latency overhead for continuous batching?
[09:59] Liam: continuous batching adds a small micro-batching wait window (tens of ms) but overall reduces GPU time per token; total p95 can improve if you reduce queueing on GPU.
[10:11] Evelyn: ok that's plausible. can we get a sample of the console metrics you show for batching and token breakdown?
[10:17] Maya: yes we'll attach screenshots of the console and a sample run.
[10:21] Tom: on compliance, Priya, can you send the SOC2 doc and the KMS integration notes?
[10:26] Priya: yes will send both.
[10:29] Zoe: anything else on your side?
[10:32] Maya: just to confirm next steps: we'll send pricing spreadsheet, security one-pager, and SE will schedule the benchmark and send harness. you'll share traffic and prompt sets.
[10:42] Evelyn: sounds good. thanks.
[10:45] [closing remarks and thanks]

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., KV cache heard as KV cash in first pass) and speaker overlaps.

End of transcript.
